endorsements.quote: Third, develop explicit liability and competency standards, including for AI- and federated-learning-mediated RPM.
Drop-out should be analysed by subgroups so that the field can detect when programmes work in aggregate but fail for the populations most in need [ 21 , 56 , 66 ].

unlisted_practices: Standardise the economic evaluation of RPM with reference frameworks specifying time horizons, perspectives (including informal-caregiver and societal), included costs, and counterfactual definitions.
Tie RPM reimbursement to the clinical work of reviewing and acting on data rather than to the device.
Establish profession-wide standards on what constitutes adequate review of asynchronous RPM data and what response times apply to which alert classes.
Treat patient privacy and benefit as design requirements, with privacy notices and data-sharing terms that are intelligible, auditable, and revisable.
Measure equity as a primary outcome of RPM implementations.

Report engagement as an outcome in RPM evaluations, including enrolment rate, active-use rate, data-transmission completeness, alert-response adherence, attrition by subgroup, and patient-reported usability and burden.
Invest in connectivity, device subsidies, multilingual interfaces, and community trust-building to implement RPM in underserved settings.

screen.reason: This is a perspective piece discussing remote patient monitoring (RPM) ecosystem challenges, including AI-mediated decision support, liability, economics, and equity, offering a policy and research agenda.
